source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: The Spectrum of Price Action: Extreme Trends to Extreme Trading Ranges

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. Helpers: range(n) = high[n]-low[n]; body(n) = close[n]-open[n]; countUp(N) = count over k in 0..N-1 of close[k] > open[k]; countDown(N) analogous; highest(x,N)[k] / lowest(x,N)[k] = extreme over N bars ending at bar k.

candidates.name: MarketInTrend
candidates.quote: the market often trends for a protracted time with only small pullbacks... An important point to remember is that the market constantly exhibits inertia and tends to continue to do what is has just been doing.
candidates.description: Primitive: approximate 'the market is in a trend' (bull side) as a net directional move over the last trendBars bars where most of those bars agree with the direction (inertia). No EMA is introduced until later chapters, so this uses only net close change plus a majority-of-bars count.

complexity.reason: 'the market is in a trend' is a design decision; net-move-plus-majority-count is one workable proxy, not Brooks's own test

notes: Later chapters define this via the 20-bar EMA; this chapter has not introduced the EMA yet.

candidates.name: MarketInTradingRange
candidates.quote: the market is moving sideways and not covering many points... an extreme trading range where every one- or two-tick up move is followed by a one- or two-tick down move and vice versa.
candidates.description: Primitive: approximate 'the market is in a trading range' as the last rangeBars bars largely overlapping (each pair's overlap at least a fraction of its range), i.e. little net progress.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..rangeBars-1: (min(high[k],high[k+1]) - max(low[k],low[k+1])) >= overlapFraction * range(k) -> inTradingRange

complexity.reason: 'trading range' is a design decision; bar-overlap is one workable proxy

notes: Same primitive family as TradingRangeContext defined in other chapters of this book; expected to merge in dedup.

candidates.name: FadeCountertrendInTrendFilter
candidates.quote: If it is in a trend, most attempts to reverse it will fail.
candidates.description: Block a long entry while the market classifies as a bear trend (MarketInTrend's short-side condition true), and mirror for shorts against a live bull trend.

candidates.name: FadeBreakoutInTradingRangeFilter
candidates.quote: If it is in a trading range, most attempts to break out into a trend will fail.
candidates.description: Block a breakout-style entry (close beyond the recent range extreme) while MarketInTradingRange is active, in either direction, since Brooks says such breakouts mostly fail.
notes: This is the filter Brooks's own preference for fading trading-range breakouts rests on; a genuine fade entry would take the opposite side once the breakout has failed (see later chapters' failed-breakout patterns).

candidates.name: PullbackLegBreakout
candidates.quote: If the market then has a second leg down and then a bar goes above the high of a prior bar, the breakout bar is a high 2. A third occurrence is a high 3, and a fourth is a high 4.
candidates.description: Primitive: within a bull trend or trading range, after exactly legCount down-legs (swing lows each lower than the one before, each followed by a failed rally), a bar closing above the high of the bar that ended the most recent down-leg is a 'high N' breakout entry.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the high of the bar that ended the most recent down-leg

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and leg counting over a variable-length window before the fixed-offset breakout test can run

notes: This is the book's core 'high 1 / high 2 / high 3 / high 4' and mirrored 'low 1 / low 2' terminology, introduced here and used throughout the trilogy; legCount is the tunable.
Brooks explicitly prefers this leg-counting label over Elliott Wave (wave 1/2/3) and over ABC/AB=CD naming; those are terminology choices, not separate mechanics.

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveSecondLegTarget
candidates.quote: Some traders who are looking for a measured move will look for a reversal back up after the second leg reaches about the same size as the first leg.
candidates.description: Exit target for a trade riding the second leg of a two-legged move: once the move from pivot C has traveled about the same distance as the first leg (pivot A to pivot B), expect a reversal and take profit near that projected level.
candidates.pseudocode: legASize = abs(priceB - priceA); target = priceC + direction * legASize * sizeMultiple; (high[0] >= target for a long)
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit at the projected measured-move level

complexity.reason: needs the three pivots (A, B, C) tracked from swing detection, not just fixed-offset bars

notes: Brooks rejects the 'AB=CD' label as inconsistent naming, but the underlying measured-move projection is the same technique used throughout the trilogy; kept as a candidate despite the naming objection.

candidates.name: TrendResumptionDayContext
candidates.quote: Whenever there is a strong trend on the open and then a tight trading range for several hours, the chances for a trend resumption day are good.
candidates.description: Session-level context filter: if the market opened with a strong trend and then entered a tight trading range for several hours, favor with-trend continuation entries in the opening trend's direction over fresh countertrend fades.

complexity.reason: session day-type classification carried forward across bars is a design decision, built on two other research-grade primitives

notes: This is a preview of the 'trend from the open' and 'trend resumption day' patterns fleshed out later in the trilogy (Part IV of this book).

candidates.name: MiddaySessionFalseBreakoutFade
candidates.quote: There is often a false breakout between approximately 11:00 a.m. and noon PST, trapping traders into the wrong direction, and that failed breakout is a great setup for a swing trade into the close.
candidates.description: During a specific mid-session time window, a breakout beyond the recent range that fails (the next bar closes back inside the range) is a fade entry, held as a swing trade toward the close.
candidates.pseudocode: Time[1] >= windowStart && Time[1] <= windowEnd && close[1] > highest(high, rangeBars)[2] && close[0] < highest(high, rangeBars)[2]
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the failed-breakout bar's low (short side of the mirror; buy stop above for the long/failed-downside-breakout case)

complexity.reason: combines a time-of-day window with a variable-offset failed-breakout scan

notes: Brooks gives PST times; the engine's session clock convention needs to be confirmed by the authoring pass.
Time window and session-specific claim make this a good candidate for a swing/reversals-book cross-reference.

rejected.quote: Whenever anyone looks at a chart, she will see areas where the market is moving diagonally and other areas where the market is moving sideways
Even the stock market crashes of 1987 and 2009 were just pullbacks to the monthly bull trend line.
rejected.reason: historical anecdote requiring monthly-chart alignment, no stated threshold

rejected.quote: When one occurs as a pullback in a trend, it is often called an ABC move... These technicians often call the pattern an AB=CD move.
rejected.reason: terminology/naming discussion, not an independent mechanical test; the underlying projection is captured in T01-06

rejected.quote: Since measured moves are an important part of trading and the AB=CD terminology is inconsistent with the more commonly used ABC labeling, the AB=CD terminology should not be used.
rejected.reason: pure naming preference, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: All trends contain smaller trading ranges, and all trading ranges contain smaller trends. Also, most trends are just parts of trading ranges on higher time frame (HTF) charts
rejected.reason: fractal/multi-timeframe claim with no stated threshold; would need higher-timeframe bar data the engine does not assemble here

chapter_summary: Short introductory chapter framing price action as a spectrum from extreme trend to extreme trading range, driven by market inertia (trends tend to continue, ranges tend to hold). Introduces the book's core leg-counting vocabulary (high 1/2/3/4, low 1/2) in place of Elliott Wave or AB=CD naming, and previews measured-move targets and 'trend from the open' / 'trend resumption day' concepts developed later. Produced two research-grade context primitives (MarketInTrend, MarketInTradingRange) reused as filters, the leg-counting breakout primitive, a measured-move exit, and two intraday day-type/time-window candidates.
